# Glossary {.unnumbered #sec-glossary}

<!-- GENERATED by scripts/build-index.R from glossary-terms.yml. Do not edit by hand. Method: planning/glossary-index-method.md -->

## Categorical Logit Model {#gl-categorical-logit-model .unnumbered .unlisted}

A regression for an outcome with several categories that have no order (also called multinomial logit). Each category except a reference one gets its own linear predictor, and the softmax turns the predictors into probabilities that are positive and add up to one.

*Think of it as:* Three doors with no order among them: each has an attractiveness for the person walking by, and the softmax turns the attractiveness into the chance of choosing each door.

*See also:* [reference category](#gl-reference-category), [independence of irrelevant alternatives](#gl-independence-of-irrelevant-alternatives)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Grading neurological deficit](ordinal-nominal-regression.qmd#ix-categorical-logit-model-1)

:::

## Category-Specific Effect {#gl-category-specific-effect .unnumbered .unlisted}

A coefficient allowed to differ from one threshold to the next (in brms, cs()). It relaxes the proportional odds assumption for one predictor, at the price of more parameters.

*Think of it as:* Letting each knot of the rope move by its own distance when the animal changes group.

*See also:* [proportional odds assumption](#gl-proportional-odds-assumption)

## Caterpillar Plot {#gl-caterpillar-plot .unnumbered .unlisted}

A plot of the estimated intercept of every group, with its credible interval, ordered from lowest to highest. It shows how much the groups differ and how sure the model is about each one.

*Think of it as:* A line of animals sorted by height, each with a measuring-error stick: you see the spread of the whole line, and which differences are bigger than the error.

*See also:* [varying intercept](#gl-varying-intercept), [shrinkage](#gl-shrinkage)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Untangling cells, sections and animals](multilevel-varying-intercepts.qmd#ix-caterpillar-plot-1); [Letting each animal have its own response](multilevel-varying-slopes.qmd#ix-caterpillar-plot-1)

:::

## Complete Pooling {#gl-complete-pooling .unnumbered .unlisted}

Estimating one value for all groups, ignoring which group a row came from. It is the model of ordinary regression when groups exist but are not modeled.

*Think of it as:* Giving every mouse the grand average as its speed.

*See also:* [no pooling](#gl-no-pooling), [partial pooling](#gl-partial-pooling)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)](multilevel-intro.qmd#ix-complete-pooling-1)

:::

## Conditional Effect {#gl-conditional-effect .unnumbered .unlisted}

The effect of a predictor in a multilevel model for a group at a given value of its varying effect, usually zero. With a log or a logit link it is the effect for the typical neuron or mouse, which is what a coefficient of a generalized multilevel model means.

*Think of it as:* The height of the median child in a class: a real child, but not the average height of the class when a few students are very tall.

*See also:* [marginal effect](#gl-marginal-effect), [varying intercept](#gl-varying-intercept)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Modeling trials within neurons and mice](multilevel-glmm.qmd#ix-conditional-effect-1)

:::

## Correlated Varying Effects {#gl-correlated-varying-effects .unnumbered .unlisted}

Two or more varying effects of the same group (for example the intercept and the slope of each mouse) modeled together as a draw from a multivariate normal distribution, with a correlation between them. In formula syntax, `(1 + x | group)`; the double bar `(1 + x || group)` sets the correlation to zero.

*Think of it as:* Two items on a restaurant bill: a table that orders expensive starters tends to order expensive mains, and a model that ignores it misjudges the tables that do both.

*See also:* [varying slope](#gl-varying-slope), [LKJ prior](#gl-lkj-prior)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Letting each animal have its own response](multilevel-varying-slopes.qmd#ix-correlated-varying-effects-1)

:::

## Credible Interval {#gl-credible-interval .unnumbered .unlisted}

A range of parameter values that holds a stated share (for example 95%) of the posterior distribution. Given the model, the data and the priors, the parameter lies inside it with that probability.

*Think of it as:* A direct statement about the effect itself: "there is a 95% probability it sits in this range". A confidence interval makes a different claim, about how often the procedure that built it captures the true value over many repetitions.

*See also:* [posterior distribution](#gl-posterior-distribution)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Why model? A first worked example](intro-applied-modeling.qmd#ix-credible-interval-1)

:::

## Crossed Grouping {#gl-crossed-grouping .unnumbered .unlisted}

A structure in which the levels of one grouping factor appear across several levels of another, such as animals each tested in every experimental block. In formula syntax, `(1 | animal) + (1 | block)`.

*Think of it as:* The rows and columns of a grid: every animal sits in every block, so neither factor lives inside the other.

*See also:* [nested grouping](#gl-nested-grouping), [grouping factor](#gl-grouping-factor)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Untangling cells, sections and animals](multilevel-varying-intercepts.qmd#ix-crossed-grouping-1)

:::

## Cumulative Logit Model {#gl-cumulative-logit-model .unnumbered .unlisted}

A regression for an ordinal outcome that supposes a hidden continuous severity, shifted by the predictors, and cut by thresholds into the grades that are observed. It models the probability of being at or below each grade (also called the proportional odds model).

*Think of it as:* A rope that nobody can see, with knots at uneven distances: the rope is the severity, each knot a cut, and the grade written down is the segment where the animal sits.

*See also:* [threshold](#gl-threshold), [proportional odds assumption](#gl-proportional-odds-assumption), [latent scale](#gl-latent-scale)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Grading neurological deficit](ordinal-nominal-regression.qmd#ix-cumulative-logit-model-1)

:::

## Design Effect {#gl-design-effect .unnumbered .unlisted}

The factor by which clustering inflates the variance of an average, $1 + (m-1)\rho$ with $m$ rows per group and $\rho$ the intraclass correlation. Dividing the number of rows by it gives the effective sample size.

*Think of it as:* Eight copies of the same photograph weigh as much as eight photographs but show one scene.

*See also:* [intraclass correlation](#gl-intraclass-correlation)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)](multilevel-intro.qmd#ix-design-effect-1) ([2](multilevel-intro.qmd#ix-design-effect-2))

:::

## Grouped Cross-Validation {#gl-grouped-cross-validation .unnumbered .unlisted}

Cross-validation whose folds hold whole groups (all the trials of a neuron, all the attempts of a mouse) out of the fit, so that the held-out data belong to groups the model has never seen. It answers "how well do I predict a new group", which ordinary leave-one-out does not.

*Think of it as:* Testing a student on a chapter they have not opened, instead of on another question from a chapter they studied with the answer key.

*See also:* [new-group prediction](#gl-new-group-prediction), [multilevel model](#gl-multilevel-model)

## Grouping Factor {#gl-grouping-factor .unnumbered .unlisted}

The column that says which group a row belongs to (mouse, neuron, patient). Its categories are the groups, and it appears after the bar in a formula such as `(1 | mouse)`.

*Think of it as:* The animal ID written on every row of the spreadsheet.

*See also:* [level](#gl-level), [varying intercept](#gl-varying-intercept)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)](multilevel-intro.qmd#ix-grouping-factor-1)

:::

## Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives {#gl-independence-of-irrelevant-alternatives .unnumbered .unlisted}

A property of the categorical logit model: the odds between two classes depend only on those two classes, not on which other classes exist. It fails when two classes are close substitutes.

*Think of it as:* Offering commuters a blue bus identical to the red one: the model would take a third of each of the car, red bus and blue bus, though in reality the two buses would just split the same riders.

*See also:* [categorical logit model](#gl-categorical-logit-model)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Grading neurological deficit](ordinal-nominal-regression.qmd#ix-independence-of-irrelevant-alternatives-1)

:::

## Intraclass Correlation {#gl-intraclass-correlation .unnumbered .unlisted}

The share of the total variance of an outcome that lies between groups instead of within them. It measures how much two rows of the same group resemble each other.

*Think of it as:* How tightly the dots of each mouse huddle around its own average compared with how far the averages of different mice are from each other.

*See also:* [design effect](#gl-design-effect), [multilevel model](#gl-multilevel-model)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Checking whether the line deserves your trust](linear-regression-assumptions.qmd#ix-intraclass-correlation-1); [The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)](multilevel-intro.qmd#ix-intraclass-correlation-1) ([2](multilevel-intro.qmd#ix-intraclass-correlation-2)); [Untangling cells, sections and animals](multilevel-varying-intercepts.qmd#ix-intraclass-correlation-1); [Modeling trials within neurons and mice](multilevel-glmm.qmd#ix-intraclass-correlation-1); [Grading neurological deficit](ordinal-nominal-regression.qmd#ix-intraclass-correlation-1)

:::

## Latent Scale {#gl-latent-scale .unnumbered .unlisted}

The scale of the linear predictor (the log of the rate, the log-odds), before the outcome is counted or flipped. Variances and intraclass correlations "on the latent scale" describe how alike the underlying rates or probabilities are, not how alike the observed counts or successes are.

*Think of it as:* How busy a bakery is on a given morning, before the luck of who happens to walk in decides how many loaves it sells.

*See also:* [intraclass correlation](#gl-intraclass-correlation), [offset](#gl-offset)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Modeling trials within neurons and mice](multilevel-glmm.qmd#ix-latent-scale-1)

:::

## Level {#gl-level .unnumbered .unlisted}

One tier of a nested data structure. Attempts sit inside mice, neurons inside patients, cells inside sections inside animals; each tier is a level.

*Think of it as:* The folders inside folders of a data drive: the file is the lowest level, the animal's folder a higher one.

*See also:* [grouping factor](#gl-grouping-factor), [multilevel model](#gl-multilevel-model)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)](multilevel-intro.qmd#ix-level-1)

:::

## Likelihood {#gl-likelihood .unnumbered .unlisted}

How probable the data you observed would be for each possible value of the parameter. It is the part of the model that carries the evidence in your data.

*Think of it as:* A detective ranking suspects by how well each one explains the clues on the table.

*See also:* [prior](#gl-prior), [posterior distribution](#gl-posterior-distribution)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Bayesian core concepts and statistical workflow](bayesian-core-workflow.qmd#ix-likelihood-1)

:::

## LKJ Prior {#gl-lkj-prior .unnumbered .unlisted}

A prior distribution for a correlation matrix, with one parameter, eta. For a single correlation its density is proportional to (1 - rho^2)^(eta - 1): eta = 1 gives every correlation the same prior weight, and larger values favor correlations near zero.

*Think of it as:* How much you believe, before seeing the data, that a baseline and a response are tied together: eta = 1 is no opinion, and a larger eta is a growing skepticism of extreme links.

*See also:* [correlated varying effects](#gl-correlated-varying-effects), [varying slope](#gl-varying-slope)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Letting each animal have its own response](multilevel-varying-slopes.qmd#ix-lkj-prior-1)

:::

## Marginal Effect {#gl-marginal-effect .unnumbered .unlisted}

The effect of a predictor averaged over the whole population of groups (neurons, mice), instead of for one group at its typical value. With an identity link it equals the conditional effect; with a log or a logit link it does not, and it is the number a reader usually has in mind.

*Think of it as:* The average height of the class, which the tall students pull above the height of the median child.

*See also:* [conditional effect](#gl-conditional-effect), [new-group prediction](#gl-new-group-prediction)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Modeling trials within neurons and mice](multilevel-glmm.qmd#ix-marginal-effect-1)

:::

## Model Expansion {#gl-model-expansion .unnumbered .unlisted}

Starting with a simple model, checking it against the data, and extending it (a more flexible shape, hierarchical structure, extra data) only where the check shows it fails.

*Think of it as:* Like adding instruments to a recording rig only when the signal you care about is not coming through, not building the whole rig on day one.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Deciding whether a line is the right model](linear-models-reflection.qmd#ix-model-expansion-1) ([2](linear-models-reflection.qmd#ix-model-expansion-2))

:::

## Multilevel Model {#gl-multilevel-model .unnumbered .unlisted}

A model in which group-level quantities (each mouse's own baseline, each neuron's own firing rate) are treated as draws from a distribution whose spread is itself a parameter learned from the data. Also called a hierarchical or mixed-effects model.

*Think of it as:* A lab that estimates each mouse's speed while also learning how much mice differ from each other, and lets that second answer decide how much each mouse's own tally is trusted.

*See also:* [partial pooling](#gl-partial-pooling), [varying intercept](#gl-varying-intercept), [shrinkage](#gl-shrinkage)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)](multilevel-intro.qmd#ix-multilevel-model-1)

:::

## Nested Grouping {#gl-nested-grouping .unnumbered .unlisted}

A structure in which every level of a lower factor belongs to one and only one level of a higher factor, such as sections inside mice. In formula syntax, `(1 | mouse/section)`, which expands to `(1 | mouse) + (1 | mouse:section)`.

*Think of it as:* Nested boxes: a slide exists only inside one box, and the slide called "Scene 1" in one mouse has nothing to do with "Scene 1" in another.

*See also:* [crossed grouping](#gl-crossed-grouping), [grouping factor](#gl-grouping-factor), [varying intercept](#gl-varying-intercept)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Untangling cells, sections and animals](multilevel-varying-intercepts.qmd#ix-nested-grouping-1)

:::

## New-Group Prediction {#gl-new-group-prediction .unnumbered .unlisted}

A prediction for a group that is not in the data (a mouse not yet tested), which adds the spread between groups to the uncertainty about the population-level line. It is wider than the interval for the average group.

*Think of it as:* The average October temperature of a city is known to a fraction of a degree, but tomorrow's temperature still varies around it by several.

*See also:* [varying slope](#gl-varying-slope), [partial pooling](#gl-partial-pooling)

## No Pooling {#gl-no-pooling .unnumbered .unlisted}

Estimating each group separately from its own rows only. It respects differences between groups but trusts thin groups completely.

*Think of it as:* Believing a mouse that has been tested twice as much as one tested nine times.

*See also:* [complete pooling](#gl-complete-pooling), [partial pooling](#gl-partial-pooling)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)](multilevel-intro.qmd#ix-no-pooling-1)

:::

## Non-Centered Parameterization {#gl-non-centered-parameterization .unnumbered .unlisted}

A way of writing a varying effect so that the sampler draws a standardized deviation and multiplies it by the group-level standard deviation, instead of drawing the group's intercept directly. It removes the funnel in the posterior that causes divergent transitions when the standard deviation is small, and it is the default of `brms`.

*Think of it as:* Measuring each group in units of the group spread instead of in absolute units, so the shape the sampler walks on no longer narrows to a neck when the spread is small.

*See also:* [varying intercept](#gl-varying-intercept), [multilevel model](#gl-multilevel-model)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Untangling cells, sections and animals](multilevel-varying-intercepts.qmd#ix-non-centered-parameterization-1); [Letting each animal have its own response](multilevel-varying-slopes.qmd#ix-non-centered-parameterization-1)

:::

## Observation-Level Random Effect {#gl-observation-level-random-effect .unnumbered .unlisted}

A varying intercept with one level per row of the data, added to a Poisson model so that each observation has its own rate. It is the lognormal-Poisson alternative to the negative binomial (a gamma-Poisson) for overdispersed counts.

*Think of it as:* Letting every single morning at the bakery have its own busyness, instead of assuming that busyness is the same all day.

*See also:* [overdispersion](#gl-overdispersion), [varying intercept](#gl-varying-intercept)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Modeling trials within neurons and mice](multilevel-glmm.qmd#ix-observation-level-random-effect-1)

:::

## Offset {#gl-offset .unnumbered .unlisted}

A term in a count model whose coefficient is fixed at 1, so that the model describes a rate (counts per unit of exposure) instead of a raw count. In a log-link model the offset is the log of the exposure.

*Think of it as:* Cell counts from sections of different sizes are not comparable until you divide by the area counted. The offset does that division inside the model.

*See also:* [overdispersion](#gl-overdispersion)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Counting cells and spikes](count-regression.qmd#ix-offset-1) ([2](count-regression.qmd#ix-offset-2))

:::

## Ordinal Outcome {#gl-ordinal-outcome .unnumbered .unlisted}

An outcome made of ordered categories (a deficit grade from 0 to 3, a clinical item scored 0 to 4): we know that a higher grade is more, but not that the step from one grade to the next is the same size everywhere.

*Think of it as:* The rungs of a ladder whose rungs are not evenly spaced: you know which rung is higher, not how far apart two rungs are.

*See also:* [cumulative logit model](#gl-cumulative-logit-model), [threshold](#gl-threshold)

## Overdispersion {#gl-overdispersion .unnumbered .unlisted}

More variability in the data than the chosen distribution allows. For a Poisson model, the variance equals the mean; overdispersion means the observed variance is clearly larger.

*Think of it as:* A model that expects every animal to behave about the same, while in reality some animals respond far more than others.

*See also:* [offset](#gl-offset)

## Partial Pooling {#gl-partial-pooling .unnumbered .unlisted}

Estimating each group as a compromise between its own data and the overall average, leaning on its own data more as the group has more of it. The balance is learned from the data through the group-level spread.

*Think of it as:* A rubber band between each mouse's own tally and the group's: a short tally is pulled harder than a long one.

*See also:* [shrinkage](#gl-shrinkage), [complete pooling](#gl-complete-pooling), [no pooling](#gl-no-pooling)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)](multilevel-intro.qmd#ix-partial-pooling-1)

:::

## Posterior Distribution {#gl-posterior-distribution .unnumbered .unlisted}

The prior updated by the data through Bayes' theorem: a full distribution showing how plausible each value of the parameter is, given the model and the data.

*Think of it as:* What is left of your hunch after you let the experiment speak. You neither discard the hunch nor ignore the data; you blend them.

*See also:* [prior](#gl-prior), [likelihood](#gl-likelihood), [credible interval](#gl-credible-interval)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Why model? A first worked example](intro-applied-modeling.qmd#ix-posterior-distribution-1)

:::

## Prior {#gl-prior .unnumbered .unlisted}

The probability distribution you give a parameter before seeing the data. It states which values you consider plausible and how strongly.

*Think of it as:* The hunch you carry into the lab before you open the results: a colleague mentioned a similar finding, or a pilot run pointed that way. It is worth something, but it is not proof.

*See also:* [posterior distribution](#gl-posterior-distribution), [likelihood](#gl-likelihood)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Why model? A first worked example](intro-applied-modeling.qmd#ix-prior-1)

:::

## Proportional Odds Assumption {#gl-proportional-odds-assumption .unnumbered .unlisted}

The assumption of the cumulative logit model that a predictor shifts the hidden severity by the same amount at every threshold, so that one coefficient describes the effect on the odds of being above any cut.

*Think of it as:* Sliding the whole rope to the right: every knot moves by the same distance.

*See also:* [cumulative logit model](#gl-cumulative-logit-model), [category-specific effect](#gl-category-specific-effect)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Grading neurological deficit](ordinal-nominal-regression.qmd#ix-proportional-odds-assumption-1)

:::

## Pseudoreplication {#gl-pseudoreplication .unnumbered .unlisted}

Analyzing repeated measurements of the same experimental unit (cells, sections or regions of one animal) as if each were an independent replicate. The apparent sample size is then larger than the number of units that were actually randomized, and the intervals are too narrow for comparisons between units.

*Think of it as:* Interviewing every member of twelve families and reporting the answers as if you had asked forty-odd unrelated people.

*See also:* [design effect](#gl-design-effect), [intraclass correlation](#gl-intraclass-correlation), [multilevel model](#gl-multilevel-model)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Untangling cells, sections and animals](multilevel-varying-intercepts.qmd#ix-pseudoreplication-1)

:::

## Reference Category {#gl-reference-category .unnumbered .unlisted}

The class of a categorical outcome whose linear predictor is fixed at zero, so that the model is identified. Every other coefficient is a log-odds against it, and changing it changes every coefficient.

*Think of it as:* The ground floor of a building: every other floor is described by how far it is above it.

*See also:* [categorical logit model](#gl-categorical-logit-model)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [Grading neurological deficit](ordinal-nominal-regression.qmd#ix-reference-category-1)

:::

## Shrinkage {#gl-shrinkage .unnumbered .unlisted}

The pull of a group's estimate toward the overall average that partial pooling produces. It is strongest for extreme estimates and for groups with little data, and it lowers the average error across groups.

*Think of it as:* The batting average after ten at-bats comes down toward the league average because part of the extreme was luck.

*See also:* [partial pooling](#gl-partial-pooling), [multilevel model](#gl-multilevel-model)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)](multilevel-intro.qmd#ix-shrinkage-1) ([2](multilevel-intro.qmd#ix-shrinkage-2))

:::

## Singular Fit {#gl-singular-fit .unnumbered .unlisted}

A maximum-likelihood fit of a multilevel model in which a group-level variance is estimated at zero, or a correlation at plus or minus 1: the estimate sits on the boundary of the allowed values because the data cannot support the covariance structure that was asked for.

*Think of it as:* Asking a survey of eight households to tell you how each household's taste in music depends on its taste in food: the answer comes out as an exact rule, which the data cannot justify.

*See also:* [correlated varying effects](#gl-correlated-varying-effects), [varying slope](#gl-varying-slope)

## Threshold {#gl-threshold .unnumbered .unlisted}

In an ordinal model, a cut point on the hidden severity scale between two neighboring grades. K grades need K minus 1 thresholds, and their spacing is estimated from the data, not assumed to be equal.

*Think of it as:* A knot in the rope: where the severity stops being grade 2 and starts being grade 3.

*See also:* [cumulative logit model](#gl-cumulative-logit-model), [ordinal outcome](#gl-ordinal-outcome)

## Varying Intercept {#gl-varying-intercept .unnumbered .unlisted}

An intercept that differs between groups, each one drawn from a common distribution. In formula syntax, `(1 | mouse)`.

*Think of it as:* Each mouse has its own baseline speed, but all baselines come from the population of mice.

*See also:* [varying slope](#gl-varying-slope), [grouping factor](#gl-grouping-factor)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)](multilevel-intro.qmd#ix-varying-intercept-1); [Untangling cells, sections and animals](multilevel-varying-intercepts.qmd#ix-varying-intercept-1) ([2](multilevel-varying-intercepts.qmd#ix-varying-intercept-2)); [Grading neurological deficit](ordinal-nominal-regression.qmd#ix-varying-intercept-1)

:::

## Varying Slope {#gl-varying-slope .unnumbered .unlisted}

A slope (an effect of a predictor) that differs between groups, drawn from a common distribution and usually correlated with the varying intercept. In formula syntax, `(1 + day | mouse)`.

*Think of it as:* Each mouse has its own rate of improving from day to day.

*See also:* [varying intercept](#gl-varying-intercept), [multilevel model](#gl-multilevel-model)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

*Where it appears:* [The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)](multilevel-intro.qmd#ix-varying-slope-1); [Letting each animal have its own response](multilevel-varying-slopes.qmd#ix-varying-slope-1)

:::
